title: FormalML: Subgoal Completion Benchmark
one_liner: FormalML is a benchmark for testing whether language models can fill in missing proof steps in formal mathematics.
lead: When mathematicians write proofs, they often skip steps and write sketches instead of complete arguments. A subgoal is one of those skipped steps—a small proof obligation left to fill in. FormalML asks: can a language model complete these steps in formal proofs, the way a mathematician's assistant would? This paper introduces the first benchmark to test this, with nearly 5,000 real problems from machine learning theory.

paras: When a mathematician writes a proof, they often skip tedious steps and write a sketch. Later, someone must fill in the gaps. This is like reading a recipe that says 'prepare the dough' without explaining how to knead it.

Language models (computer programs that predict words) have gotten good at theorem proving—writing formal proofs the computer can verify. But no one had tested whether they can do the real assistant job: taking a human sketch and filling in the one or two missing steps. A language model needs to retrieve the right facts from earlier in the proof, understand what still needs proving, and write a convincing argument. Each is hard alone; together, they are much harder.

callout.html: FormalML creates 4,937 real subgoal completion problems from machine learning theory, tests today's best language models on them, and finds they still fail on most of them.

steps.b: Extract real problems from Lean code
steps.text: Starting with machine learning theory proofs written in Lean (a formal language), extract every gap left between two consecutive steps.
Use a translation tactic to rewrite imperative proofs (do X, then Y) into declarative form (X is true because...).
Collect subgoal completion problems spanning optimization theory and probability inequalities, marked by difficulty level.

steps.b: Test language models on premise retrieval
steps.text: Ask models to pick which earlier facts matter most for closing each gap (the harder part, because the proof can be long).
Check whether the model's completed proof is correct (verified by Lean), and how much computation it took.

paras: The paper creates a new benchmark—a collection of test problems—and runs existing language models on them. The benchmark itself is the contribution. The benchmark object is a subgoal: a small formal proof obligation plus the surrounding context (the facts the model can use) and the goal statement.

hidden.h2: The gap between sketch and proof
hidden.name: step complexity in formal proofs
paras: Every step in a formal proof requires evidence. Evidence lives in the context—the definitions, lemmas, and earlier results the mathematician can invoke. The hidden quantity here is how many context facts exist, and how obvious it is which ones matter for filling the current gap.

The paper measures this by counting the size of each proof context and tracking which facts the model retrieves (picks as relevant). If a context has 200 facts and the model must pick the three that actually matter, that is a hard retrieval task. The paper tests this with real research-level machine learning proofs, where contexts are large and the connections are subtle.

heat.caption: Darker means the model judged a fact as relevant to the current goal. The model must pick the right ones (marked with a box).

reads.html: To fill a gap in a proof, you need to know which earlier facts to use. A long proof means many facts to search through. The benchmark tests whether models can find the needles in the haystack.

Premise retrieval (picking relevant facts) is part of the benchmark. The paper emphasizes that combining retrieval with subgoal completion is new and hard—existing benchmarks test one or the other, but not both together.

paras: A subgoal completion task requires the language model to do three things at once. First, it must retrieve: scan the proof context and identify which earlier facts are relevant to the current goal. This is like finding the right facts in a library when the library catalog is partial. Second, it must understand: read the goal statement in formal notation and grasp what counts as a valid proof. Third, it must generate: write a formal argument that Lean will accept as correct.

The benchmark is hard because these three tasks interfere. Retrieving too many facts buries the signal in noise. Retrieving too few facts starves the model of the information it needs. The model must balance precision and recall—a trade-off that formal proofs make especially sharp, because Lean accepts only correct proofs, not nearly correct ones.

math.words: accuracy = (number of subgoals completed correctly) / (total subgoals)
symbols: total number of subgoals in the benchmark
the proof the model generates for subgoal i
Lean formally checks and accepts the proof (1) or rejects it (0)
accuracy: the fraction of subgoals the model completes correctly

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Lean accepts 62 of them (verified correct), rejects 38.
Accuracy = 62 / 100 = 62%. The model solved 62 percent of the gaps.

math.note: Lean is not forgiving—a proof is either correct or it is not. So accuracy is a binary per-problem: either the model's completion verified, or it did not.

charts.title: Without premise retrieval
charts.note: Models guess at which context facts matter, often picking the wrong ones.

charts.title: With premise retrieval
charts.note: Learning to retrieve facts helps, because the model spends less effort guessing which context facts matter and more effort on writing the proof. Hard goals remain difficult because some proof techniques are not shown anywhere in the context.

items.html: A long proof means many facts to consider. The model may forget which ones matter, especially if a key fact appears early or late in the context.
In Lean, a single typo makes the proof invalid. Models trained on English text often write nearly correct proofs that fail formal verification by one character.
Some subgoals need a proof technique that is not explicitly shown elsewhere in the context. The model must infer or generalize. This is rare in easy benchmarks but common in research proofs.

A good model learns to retrieve sparingly (only the most relevant facts), follow formal syntax precisely, and apply known techniques to new goals. FormalML lets researchers measure progress on all three at once.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Write a small language model (or use an existing one) and test it on a subset of FormalML. The demo should show: (1) how many subgoals it completes correctly (accuracy); (2) which types of problems it solves (simple, medium, hard, by topic); (3) which context facts it retrieves (does it pick the right ones?). Measure both accuracy and the cost (how much computation time or API calls it took).
demo.metric_eq: accuracy_by_difficulty = {easy: 70%, medium: 35%, hard: 5%}; efficiency = avg time per subgoal
demo.closing: The demo must make clear that even the best models today struggle when proofs are long, formal syntax is strict, and the required proof technique is not obvious.
